scenes.title: hook: a table older than the electron

voiceover.text: Here's something strange. Mendeleev arranged the elements in eighteen sixty-nine, by grouping elements with similar properties. The electron wasn't discovered until eighteen ninety-seven. Yet look at the modern table's shape. The left block is two columns wide, the middle block is ten, and the right block is six. Those are exactly the capacities of the s, d and p subshells. Let's see how.

Start with the rows, called periods. An element's period number is its highest occupied energy level, its outer shell. Across period three, from sodium to argon, every element is filling level three, first three s, then three p. Sodium ends in three s one. Argon ends in three p six, with level three's s and p both full. Then potassium puts its next electron into level four, and a new period begins.

Now the blocks. An element's block tells you the type of subshell its last electron went into. The two columns on the left are the s block. The six on the right are the p block. The ten in the middle are the d block, and the two separate rows underneath are the f block, fourteen wide. That's why the table has this shape. Each block is as wide as the number of electrons its subshell can hold.

The columns are groups, and this is where the pattern really pays off. Valence electrons are the electrons in the outer shell. Down group one, lithium ends in two s one, sodium in three s one, and potassium in four s one. Different levels, but always one valence electron, in an s subshell. Down group seventeen, every element ends in s two, p five, so seven valence electrons. For groups one and two, the number of valence electrons equals the group number. For groups thirteen to eighteen, subtract ten. Helium has two.
Quick prediction. An atom has the configuration one s two, two s two, two p six, three s two, three p six, four s two. Which period, and which group is it in?

scenes.title: reading it, and a classic trap

voiceover.text: Period four, because its highest level is four. Group two, because it has two valence electrons, in an s subshell. It's calcium. Here's a classic trap. An element with six valence electrons isn't in group six. Group six is in the d block. Six valence electrons, s two p four, puts it in group sixteen.

Here's why groups matter so much. A chemical property describes how a substance reacts to form new substances. A physical property can be observed without making a new substance, like state, colour, or conductivity. Elements in a group share their valence arrangement, so they react in similar ways. Every group one metal reacts with water, making hydrogen gas and an alkaline solution. The halogens in group seventeen are all reactive non-metals, made of pairs of atoms. And the noble gases, with a full outer shell, hardly react at all.

Position also tells us about physical properties. Metals sit on the left and in the middle, with just a few valence electrons. They're shiny, they conduct heat and electricity, and they're malleable, which means they can be hammered into shape. Non-metals sit at the top right. As solids they're dull and brittle, they don't conduct electricity, and many are gases. Along the staircase between them are the metalloids, like silicon. Silicon is shiny like a metal, but brittle like a non-metal, and it conducts electricity only a little. That's why it's used in computer chips.

scenes.title: across period three at room temperature

voiceover.text: Let's walk across period three at room temperature. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are solid metals. Silicon is a solid metalloid. Phosphorus and sulfur are solid non-metals. Then chlorine is a pale green gas, and argon is a colourless gas. So across a period, elements change from metals to non-metals. And across the whole table, only eleven elements are gases at room temperature, and only two are liquids, bromine and mercury. All the rest are solids.

scenes.title: a surprise: one group, three states

voiceover.text: Here's a surprise. The halogens share their chemistry, but not their state. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, and iodine is a solid. Same valence arrangement, different states. Explaining that needs the forces between molecules, which come later in this module. So a group shares its chemistry, but not every physical property.
So here's the map. Row, outer shell. Column, outer electrons. Block, last subshell. Read those from a configuration, and you can place any element, and predict how it behaves.

Your turn. Selenium has atomic number thirty-four. Write its electron configuration, then state its period, group and block. Name one element with similar chemical properties, and explain why. Pause here to answer.

Selenium is argon, three d ten, four s two, four p four. Its highest level is four, so it's in period four. Its outer shell holds four s two, four p four, which is six valence electrons. The full three d isn't in the outer shell. So it's group sixteen, in the p block. Sulfur, or oxygen, has similar chemistry, because it has the same outer arrangement, s two p four. Putting it in group six is the classic slip.

Last one. Three elements are described by their properties. A is shiny, conducts electricity well, can be hammered into shape, and melts at six hundred and sixty degrees. B is yellow and brittle, doesn't conduct, and melts at a hundred and fifteen degrees. C is shiny grey and brittle, conducts slightly, and melts at fourteen hundred and fourteen degrees. Classify each, and say where each type is found in the periodic table. Pause here to answer.

A is a metal. It's shiny, conducts well and is malleable, and metals sit on the left and in the middle. B is a non-metal. It's brittle and doesn't conduct, and non-metals sit at the top right. C is a metalloid, shiny but brittle, and only slightly conducting, so it sits on the staircase. Calling C a metal, just because it's shiny, is the classic slip. Brittleness and weak conduction say metalloid.

So electron arrangements organise the whole table. The period gives the outer shell, the group gives the valence electrons, and the block gives the last subshell. Now, think about size. Sodium and chlorine both have three shells. Are they the same size? And potassium has one more shell than sodium. Next, why does atomic radius change across a period and down a group?
